failures.title: Audi CJEB Engine Problems - What Actually Fails

items.title: Timing Chain Stretch & Tensioner Failure - 2012-2015 (Early Gen 3 / Late Gen 2 carryover)
items.whatHappens: The EA888 architecture is prone to timing chain stretch and tensioner failure, particularly on earlier production runs of the CJEB. Symptoms include a distinct rattling noise on cold starts, check engine lights, and eventually catastrophic engine interference if the chain snaps or jumps teeth.
items.repairVsReplace: If caught early, a timing chain and tensioner replacement is possible. However, if the chain has jumped and damaged valves or pistons, a full CJEB engine replacement is required to prevent further destruction.

items.title: Water Pump & Thermostat Housing Leaks - 2012-2018
items.whatHappens: The plastic water pump and integrated thermostat housing are prone to cracking and leaking coolant over time. This leads to low coolant warnings, overheating, and potential head gasket damage if the engine is repeatedly run hot.
items.repairVsReplace: This is a well-understood repair; replacing the water pump and thermostat housing with updated aluminium or revised plastic units resolves the issue without requiring a full engine replacement, provided overheating hasn't warped the cylinder head.

items.title: Carbon Buildup on Intake Valves - 2012-2018
items.whatHappens: As a direct-injection engine, the CJEB does not wash fuel over the intake valves, leading to severe carbon buildup over time. This restricts airflow, causing rough idling, misfires, and reduced performance.
items.repairVsReplace: A professional walnut blasting or chemical carbon clean restores performance. It is a maintenance item rather than a fatal engine failure, but severe neglect can lead to valve seat damage.

failures.goodYearsLine: Post-2015 CJEB units (Gen 3 revision) received an updated timing chain tensioner and improved water pump design, significantly reducing the incidence of these failures compared to the 2012-2014 production run .

variants.intro: The CJEB engine code is stamped on a label located in the engine bay (typically on the timing belt cover or strut tower) and is clearly listed on your vehicle’s V5C registration document under "Engine Number". It can also be definitively verified via a VIN decode.

buyingGuide.title: Buying a Replacement CJEB - What to Choose

options.label: Used
options.body: A used CJEB is only advisable if it comes with a comprehensive service history proving the timing chain tensioner and water pump have already been replaced with updated units. Given the known EA888 weaknesses, a low-mileage used unit without documented preventative maintenance carries a high risk of immediate repeat failure. Compare used CJEB engines

options.label: Reconditioned
options.body: This is the highly recommended route for the CJEB. A proper reconditioning process will address the engine's known weaknesses by fitting an updated timing chain tensioner, installing a revised water pump and thermostat housing, and performing a carbon clean on the intake valves, delivering near-new reliability without the premium of a brand-new unit. Compare reconditioned CJEB engines

options.label: Rebuilt
options.body: A full rebuild is justified if the CJEB has suffered catastrophic timing chain failure that bent valves or damaged pistons, or if the vehicle is a high-value Audi Q5 or A5 intended for long-term ownership. An upgraded rebuild should include reinforced timing components and an aluminium water pump upgrade. Compare rebuilt CJEB engines

buyingGuide.supplyFitLine: Securing a CJEB through our network guarantees a minimum 12-month warranty, with nationwide delivery and the option for vetted local specialist fitting to ensure the job is done right the first time. Explore supply and fit options
buyingGuide.vehicleValueNote: For typical host vehicles like the Audi A4 B8/B9, A5 8T/F5, and Q5 8R/FY, current UK market values range from £4,000 to £18,000. A reconditioned CJEB replacement (£2,000-£3,800 supply-only) represents a financially viable investment for most examples. However, if the lowest viable replacement cost exceeds approximately 60% of the vehicle's current market value (common on sub-£4k early B8 or 8R examples), evaluate scrap value before committing.
